title: Database Indexing, B-Trees, and Query Plan Optimization
description: Master indexing mechanics: B-tree indexed lookup, composite indexes, column order, write cost overhead, EXPLAIN query plan analysis, and index trade-offs.
learning_objectives: Explain internal B-tree index structures and contrast indexed lookup against full sequential table scans
Design composite indexes adhering to the leftmost prefix rule and optimal column order
Evaluate index trade-offs including storage footprint and mutation write cost on INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE
Analyze query execution performance using EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE to inspect query plan operations

sections.title: B-tree mechanics: Indexed lookup vs sequential scan
sections.learning_objective: Understand how B-tree indexes accelerate search from O(N) to O(log N).
sections.markdown: A database index is an auxiliary data structure that accelerates data retrieval. The default and most versatile index type in PostgreSQL is the balanced tree (`B-tree`). Without an index, finding a row requires a sequential scan (`Seq Scan`), reading every disk page in the table in $O(N)$ time. A `B-tree` index organizes sorted keys in a multi-level balanced tree, enabling an `indexed lookup` in $O(\log N)$ disk page accesses. The leaf nodes contain pointers (tuple IDs or TIDs) pointing directly to physical table heap pages.

examples.explanation: Creates a B-tree index on the email column, enabling instant log-time lookups.

key_points: B-tree indexes maintain balanced sorted keys, supporting equality and range queries (<, <=, =, >=, >).
Indexed lookups navigate from root to leaf in O(log N) page reads, bypassing full table scans.
sections.checkpoint: Why are B-tree indexes suitable for both equality (=) and range (<, BETWEEN) operators?

sections.title: Composite indexes: Leftmost prefix rule and column order
sections.learning_objective: Construct composite indexes taking column order and query patterns into account.
sections.markdown: A `composite index` (or multicolumn index) indexes multiple columns together: `CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_date ON orders (customer_id, order_date)`. The `column order` is critical due to the leftmost prefix rule. Keys are sorted primarily by the first column, and secondarily by the second column. As a result, this index can accelerate queries filtering on `customer_id` alone, or `customer_id` AND `order_date`. However, it cannot be used efficiently for a query filtering only on `order_date` without `customer_id`!

examples.explanation: Optimizes a multi-attribute filter using a single composite index.

key_points: The leftmost prefix rule requires queries to filter on the leading columns of a composite index.
Place the column with highest equality filter frequency as the first column in the index definition.
sections.checkpoint: Can an index on (A, B, C) be used for a query WHERE B = 5 AND C = 10? Why or why not?

sections.title: Index trade-offs: Query acceleration vs write cost
sections.learning_objective: Quantify storage overhead and write amplification caused by excessive indexing.
sections.markdown: While indexes accelerate SELECT queries, they are not free. Every index introduces significant `index trade-offs`. First is the `write cost`: whenever you perform an `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE`, PostgreSQL must update not only the base table heap, but also every single index on that table. If a table has 10 indexes, a single row insertion results in 11 separate write operations, increasing disk I/O, write-ahead logging (WAL), and lock contention. Second, indexes consume substantial RAM (buffer cache) and disk space.

examples.code:
-- Inspecting index sizes in PostgreSQL
SELECT relname AS index_name, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS index_size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE relname = 'idx_orders_cust_date';
examples.explanation: Monitors disk usage of secondary indexes to prevent bloated storage costs.

key_points: Indexes speed up reads but penalize writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE write cost).
Unused or duplicate indexes waste RAM buffer cache and degrade database throughput.
sections.checkpoint: What happens to indexes when you UPDATE a column that is NOT included in any index? (Hint: HOT updates)

sections.title: Query plan analysis: EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE
sections.learning_objective: Interpret query execution plans to identify scans, joins, and bottlenecks.
sections.markdown: To see whether the PostgreSQL optimizer actually uses your index, run `EXPLAIN` before your query. `EXPLAIN` outputs the estimated `query plan` produced by the cost-based optimizer without running the query. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the query, outputting real execution times, buffer cache hits, and row counts. Key plan nodes include: `Seq Scan` (full table read), `Index Scan` (navigates index then fetches heap row), `Index Only Scan` (all needed columns exist inside index leaves, zero heap fetches!), and `Bitmap Index Scan` (gathers heap page locations before bulk fetching).

examples.code:
-- Inspect execution plan for customer order query
EXPLAIN SELECT id, total_amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 101;
examples.explanation: Generates the query plan revealing whether an Index Scan or Seq Scan is scheduled.
examples.expected_output:
Index Scan using idx_orders_cust_date on orders  (cost=0.15..8.17 rows=1 width=36)
  Index Cond: (customer_id = 101)

key_points: EXPLAIN displays the estimated optimizer cost and execution nodes without executing the query.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query to report actual execution time in milliseconds and memory usage.
Index Only Scan is the highest-performance access method, reading zero heap pages.
sections.checkpoint: What causes the optimizer to pick a Seq Scan over an Index Scan even when an index exists on the column?

sections.title: Index optimization interview check and practice
sections.learning_objective: Solve database performance tuning and indexing interview scenarios.
sections.markdown:
Indexing and query optimization questions appear in nearly all senior backend and database engineering interviews.

### Core Interview Questions
1. *Why doesn't the database use an index when you write `WHERE UPPER(email) = 'ALICE@EXAMPLE.COM'`?*
   *(Because the index stores raw email strings, not the evaluated function result. The engine must evaluate UPPER() on every row, forcing a full Seq Scan. Fix: create an expression/functional index `CREATE INDEX idx_upper_email ON customers (UPPER(email))`)*. 
2. *What is an Index Only Scan, and what is the `COVERING` or `INCLUDE` clause?*
   *(An Index Only Scan satisfies the entire query from the index leaves without touching the table heap. The `INCLUDE` clause adds payload columns to index leaf pages without sorting on them).* 
3. *Why should you index foreign key columns?*
   *(PostgreSQL does NOT automatically index foreign keys. Without an index on the child table's foreign key, deleting a row in the parent table forces a sequential scan across the child table to check for orphans!)* 

### Arena Practice Problems
- `sql-optimize-slow-query`: Replacing Seq Scan with composite index
- `sql-covering-index-design`: Crafting an Index Only Scan using INCLUDE
- `sql-foreign-key-indexing`: Preventing cascade deletion table locks with FK indexes

examples.explanation: Demonstrates an expression index that enables indexed lookup on transformed predicates.
examples.expected_output:
Bitmap Heap Scan on customers ...
  Recheck Cond: (upper((email)::text) = 'ALICE@EXAMPLE.COM'::text)

key_points: Always check for unindexed foreign keys in child tables.
Avoid wrapping indexed columns in functions within WHERE clauses unless you use functional indexes.
sections.checkpoint: Why is indexing a boolean column with a 50/50 distribution almost always useless to the optimizer?

summary: B-tree indexes accelerate searches from O(N) sequential scans down to O(log N) indexed lookups.
Composite indexes must be designed around the leftmost prefix rule and query column order.
Indexes involve direct engineering trade-offs: faster reads vs higher write cost on mutations and disk space.
EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveal the optimizer query plan: Seq Scan, Index Scan, and Index Only Scan.
Foreign key columns must be indexed manually in PostgreSQL to prevent full table scans during parent deletes.
interview_takeaways: In performance interviews, immediately mention EXPLAIN ANALYZE to identify sequential scans.
Explain the leftmost prefix rule and why column ordering in composite indexes matters.
Remind interviewers that wrapping columns in functions (e.g. UPPER(col)) invalidates standard B-tree indexes.
common_mistakes: Applying functions to indexed columns in WHERE predicates (e.g. WHERE YEAR(date) = 2026), disabling the index
Forgetting to create indexes on foreign key columns, causing parent DELETE operations to freeze
Over-indexing tables with 15+ indexes, causing insert and update throughput to collapse
Assuming PostgreSQL automatically uses an index for low-cardinality columns (e.g. boolean flags)
